summary: Stamford Harbor Ledge Light, a cast-iron tower on a caisson lit in 1882, was discontinued in 1953, passed through private owners, and is being restored by a nonprofit.

light.note: As first lit: fixed red fourth-order light, focal plane 60 ft (18.3 m), visible 11 1/4 nautical miles (nomination; Board notice quoted by LighthouseFriends). Today per Rowlett: white flash every 4 s, focal plane 80 ft (24.5 m); whether it is shown now is not settled (see notes).

lens.note: Original fourth-order Fresnel lens (nomination). Rowlett lists a 200 mm lens in the tower today.

structures.note: Rowlett: 60 ft (18 m) tower on a cast-iron caisson 30 ft across (nomination: caisson 30 ft across, 28 ft high; superstructure 49 ft).

access.note: Privately owned (nomination). Accessible only by boat; site and tower closed (Rowlett).

facts.agency: Private owner; Stamford Harbor Lighthouse Project (site manager, per Rowlett)

events.note: Board officials visit and recommend a day beacon on the ledge and a lighted beacon across the channel (not built)
Congress appropriates $30,000 for a lighthouse; site chosen at Chatham Rocks
Tower and caisson built (cast-iron sections from a Boston foundry, bolted together on site)
Fixed red fourth-order light exhibited from 10 February 1882 (Board notice, as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Original fourth-order Fresnel lens; fixed red
Keeper Cook's launch fails in a storm on the way back; his mother-in-law keeps the light for two nights
27 August: light out and keeper unable to land in high seas; three Stamford yachtsmen restore the light by 1 a.m.
Keeper Raymond F. Bliven drowned in August 1931 (ruled accidental); the light went out the following night
A fog signal is added; assistant keepers assigned and head keeper's family no longer allowed at the station
2 October 1939: keeper Martin L. Sowle rescues one of two civilians whose boat swamped; medal awarded 1940
Discontinued by the government; property offered for sale
Three Stamford men buy the abandoned tower at auction for $10,100
Tower auctioned for $230,000 to a private owner; later owners follow
Bought for $500,000 by two men who form the nonprofit Stamford Harbor Lighthouse Project
Structural restoration begins (Rowlett); work continuing in 2026. The site was secured and debris removed in 2024.
Launch disabled while Keeper Cook and his wife returned to the light; Eatons Neck lifesaving crew rescued the couple at daybreak (LighthouseFriends, from a 1908 newspaper)

keepers.name: Laura Weickman
keepers.note: Mother-in-law of Keeper John J. Cook; kept the light burning alone for two nights during the 1908 storm, while Cook was stranded (LighthouseFriends). Not on the USLHS roster.

wrecks.vessel: Keeper Cook's launch (with his wife aboard)
wrecks.outcome: Engine failed and the boat drifted onto rocks; oar lost; rescued by Eatons Neck lifesaving crew after a night adrift
Swamped and sank while removing can buoys; Keeper Martin L. Sowle rescued one man from a spar in a 16-foot dory; the second man's body was recovered a week later

corrections.why: 18.3 m (60 ft) is the 1882 focal plane (nomination, from a 19th-century chart). Rowlett's directory gives the focal plane today as 80 ft (24.5 m). The record's figure should be marked as the original, or changed to the current figure after checking the Coast Guard light list.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Not a contradiction: the nomination gives 60 ft from a 19th-century chart (1882 light); Rowlett gives 80 ft for the light today. The record's 18.3 m is the 1882 figure.

The nomination says only that the light passed through a number of owners. LighthouseFriends gives a city transfer, a return to the government, a 1967 auction and a 1984 auction. Wikipedia's lead says the light was sold to a private party in 1955; that date is not confirmed by any source read and is not used.

The nomination describes a mechanically struck bell from the start (every 2 seconds). LighthouseFriends says a fog signal was added in 1937. Both may be right (a bell, then a powered signal), but the sources do not describe the 1937 signal.

notes_for_editor: Status is open: the record says active and notes that sources differ on whether the light is still lit. Rowlett says reactivated in 1985 with a white flash every 4 s and an 80 ft focal plane; the 1991 nomination describes only a small privately maintained beacon on the lantern roof; the record's characteristic Fl W 4s is Rowlett's. Please check the Coast Guard light list before stating that the light is shown. Wikipedia's infobox and lead were consulted only as leads: they give 'deactivated 1953-1985', 'lens 200 mm (current)' and 'sold to a private party in 1955'. The 1955 sale is not confirmed by any source read here and conflicts with LighthouseFriends's city transfer and 1967 auction; it is left out. Range: the record's 6.0 nm is not supported by any source read; the 11 1/4 nm in the story is the original nomination figure. Height: the record's 20.6 m is not supported; Rowlett gives 60 ft (18 m) for the tower, and the nomination gives a 49 ft superstructure on a 28 ft caisson. No Board report for 1882-1893 is in the local corpus, so the 1882 opening date rests on LighthouseFriends quoting the Board's notice. The 1894 oil-house item (scan page 378) may refer to the light or to another Stamford Harbor structure; the story says only 'at Stamford Harbor'. The 1908 interview quotation is LighthouseFriends's transcription of a 1908 newspaper that LighthouseFriends does not name; a newspaper search could identify it, and none was made here. The 1931 death and the 1939 rescue are recounted from LighthouseFriends, which in turn cites Coast Guard and newspaper sources; neither was checked. Private people are not named: the 1984 owner and the civilians in the 1939 rescue; the 2023 buyers are named because they publicly lead the nonprofit. Laura Weickman is named as a family member who kept the light for two nights in 1908. Roster stints are copied from the USLHS place record with its person slugs; the 'USCG' heading is the archive's. No newspaper search was run for this station. Checked this pass: the first draft's 'about 0.6 nautical miles' was a conversion of the sources' 'two-thirds of a mile' and has been removed; the 'Western Connecticut Planning Region' and 'opens to Long Island Sound' phrases were not in any source read and have been removed. The 2008 and 2020 market dates come from LighthouseFriends (2008) and Rowlett (2020, $1.595 million); the draft had wrongly attributed 2020 to LighthouseFriends. The 1908 rescue by the Eatons Neck lifesaving crew (LighthouseFriends) was left out of the first draft and is now in the story. The 1913 and 1939 accounts are LighthouseFriends paraphrases of Coast Guard and newspaper material; not checked against those originals. The 1937 fog signal: both the nomination and LighthouseFriends describe a machine-struck fog bell from 1882, so the story says the sources do not make clear what was added in 1937. The Board's fiscal 1894 'Stamford Harbor' entry (item 260) is read as the light; the next entry (Pine Island) is a different structure. The 1934 and 1937 keeper roster headings are the archive's own. The 1927 Hazel Iten incident in LighthouseFriends involves private people and is left out. The 2023 buyers are named only for their public roles as leads of the nonprofit; the 1984 owner and the 1939 civilians are not named. Wording pass: about 23 sentences were reworded where they followed LighthouseFriends, NRHP or Rowlett wording closely; the Coast Guard medal and 'long list of instances' quotations were turned into paraphrase. One short LighthouseFriends quotation remains ('And that light up aloft is a sermon in itself'), the single short quotation allowed from that copyrighted source.
